title: Docker on a VPS
subtitle: Run containerized apps on your own server with Docker Compose, auto-updating containers, and Nginx proxying

content.text: Docker Compose on a VPS combines the best of both worlds: the reproducibility and isolation of containers with the simplicity and cost of a single VPS. You get the same docker-compose.yml that runs locally to also run in production. No Kubernetes. No ECS. One file describes your entire stack — app, database, Redis, worker — and a single command starts everything.

content.code:
# Install Docker via the official script (simplest method)
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh

# Add your user to the docker group (avoids sudo for docker commands)
sudo usermod -aG docker deploy
newgrp docker  # apply group change without logout

# Verify
docker --version   # Docker 27.x.x
docker compose version  # Docker Compose v2.x.x

# Docker Compose v2 is built into Docker — no separate install needed
# Use 'docker compose' (with a space) not 'docker-compose' (hyphen)

services:
  app:
    image: ghcr.io/myorg/myapp:latest  # Pull from GitHub Container Registry
    restart: always
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/myapp
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    # Don't expose port externally — Nginx proxies to it
    expose:
      - "3000"
    networks:
      - app-net

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: myapp
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - app-net

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    networks:
      - app-net

networks:
  app-net:
    driver: bridge

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:

# Clone repo to server
git clone https://github.com/myorg/myapp.git /home/deploy/myapp
cd /home/deploy/myapp

# Create .env file with secrets (NEVER commit this)
cat > .env << 'EOF'
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=supersecretpassword
JWT_SECRET=anothersecretvalue
EOF
chmod 600 .env

# Start the stack
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d

# View logs
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml logs -f app

# Run database migrations (one-off command)
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml exec app npm run db:migrate

# Update to latest image
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml pull
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d
# Docker Compose performs a rolling update (stops old, starts new)

# View running containers
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml ps

# In docker-compose.prod.yml, expose the app to localhost only:
services:
  app:
    image: ghcr.io/myorg/myapp:latest
    ports:
      # Bind to 127.0.0.1 — only Nginx on this host can reach port 3000
      # 0.0.0.0:3000:3000 would expose it to the internet (don't do this)
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    # ... rest of config

services:
  # ... your existing services ...

  watchtower:
    image: containrrr/watchtower
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      # If pulling from GitHub Container Registry:
      - /home/deploy/.docker/config.json:/config.json
    environment:
      WATCHTOWER_POLL_INTERVAL: 300      # check every 5 minutes
      WATCHTOWER_CLEANUP: "true"         # remove old images
      WATCHTOWER_INCLUDE_STOPPED: "false"
      WATCHTOWER_NOTIFICATIONS: "email"  # optional notifications
    command: --interval 300 app           # only watch the 'app' service

content.text: Use Watchtower only for services where instant updates are safe. For databases and stateful services, update manually so you can run migrations first. For your application container, Watchtower is great — it detects when a new image is pushed to the registry and redeploys automatically. Combined with your CI/CD pipeline pushing to GitHub Container Registry on every merge, you get automatic deploys to your VPS without any extra orchestration.

questions.question: In the docker-compose.prod.yml above, the app service uses 'expose: ["3000"]' not 'ports: ["3000:3000"]'. What's the difference?
options: No difference — both make port 3000 accessible the same way
'expose' documents the port but doesn't publish it outside Docker's network; 'ports' publishes to the host — required for Nginx to reach it from outside the container network
'expose' is for HTTP only; 'ports' supports all protocols
questions.explanation: 'expose' only makes the port accessible to OTHER containers on the same Docker network — not to the host machine or the internet. It's useful for inter-container communication when your proxy (Nginx) also runs as a container (in which case it can reach the app via container name on the Docker network). In our setup, Nginx runs directly on the host (not in Docker), so we actually need 'ports: ["127.0.0.1:3000:3000"]' to expose the port to the host — but bound to 127.0.0.1 only, preventing direct internet access.

faq.q: Should I run Nginx in Docker too, or on the host?
faq.a: Either works. Running Nginx on the host is simpler for beginners — Certbot can manage certificates directly. Running Nginx in Docker (with jwilder/nginx-proxy or Traefik) is more portable. For a single VPS, host-installed Nginx is less moving parts. For multiple apps on the same VPS, Traefik as a reverse proxy container that auto-discovers other containers and handles SSL is worth learning.

examples: Many self-hosted tools (Plausible Analytics, Umami, Gitea, Mattermost) are designed to run on a VPS with Docker Compose. Their documentation gives you a docker-compose.yml and you're live in 10 minutes
The 'Ship Your App' movement popularized by Kamal and Rails showed that Docker on a single VPS can handle significant traffic. Prime Day-scale? No. 10,000 daily active users? Absolutely
